ex.en: My Korean ability improved.

좋아지다.nuance: 좋아지다 is the adjective 좋다 (good) plus -아지다, the pattern that turns a state-word into 'become that state', so it literally means 'come to be good' — a gradual drift from worse to better, not a fixed quality. The key contrast is 좋다 vs 좋아지다: 좋다 just says something IS good right now (기분이 좋아요 = I feel good), while 좋아지다 reports a CHANGE toward good (기분이 좋아졌어요 = I feel better than before). It is warm and neutral in register, fine in both 반말 and 존댓말, and shows up constantly with 몸(body), 기분(mood), 날씨(weather), 사이(relationship), and 실력(skill). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 좋다 when you really mean a transition — 'My Korean got better' is 좋아졌어요, never 좋았어요, because 좋았어요 just means 'it was good (in the past)'. Note too that 좋아지다 means 'come to like' when the subject is a person feeling (그 사람이 좋아졌어요 = I came to like that person), so context decides between 'get better' and 'grow fond of'.
좋아지다.explanation: 좋아지다 (joajida) = "to get better". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 좋아져요 plus one useful sentence like 기분이 좋아졌어요 ("My mood got better"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 좋아지고 싶어요 for what you want, 좋아질 수 있어요 for what you can, 좋아질 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
좋아지다.shortExplanation: 좋아지다 means "to get better" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 좋아지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 좋아져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 기분이 좋았어요 to mean 'my mood improved' — 좋았어요 only means 'I felt good (back then)' with no sense of change; for the improvement you need 좋아졌어요.
Treating 좋아지다 like a normal adjective and trying 좋아지다예요 — it is a verb (좋다 + 아지다), so the present is 좋아져요, never *좋아지다예요.

Using 좋아지다 for someone improving a thing on purpose; 좋아지다 is intransitive (it happens by itself). To say 'I improved my grades' you act on them with a different verb — 좋아지다 only describes the grades themselves getting better.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 좋아지다 becomes 좋아질 수 있어요 ("can") and 좋아질 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Very common about feelings and health

examples.en: The weather got better
examples.note: Simple weather change, past tense

examples.en: My condition is getting better these days
examples.note: -고 있어요 shows the change is ongoing

examples.en: After taking medicine my body got a lot better
examples.note: -으니까 gives the cause of the improvement

ex.en: The meeting time changed to three.

바뀌다.nuance: 바뀌다 is the intransitive twin of 바꾸다: the thing that changes is itself the subject (이/가) and nobody is named as the doer, so it covers things getting switched, replaced, or mixed up on their own. The dividing line vs 변하다 is key — 변하다 means a thing's inner nature transforms (사람이 변했다 = he's become a different person), while 바뀌다 means one item is swapped out for another (번호가 바뀌었다 = the number was replaced). Use 바꾸다 when YOU actively swap something (번호를 바꿨어요) and 바뀌다 when it simply ends up different (번호가 바뀌었어요). The 요-form is 바뀌어요 because the stem ends in the vowel 위, which won't contract — so spelling matters: it's 바뀌-, and the polite past is 바뀌었어요, never the wrong 바껴요/바꼈어요 that English speakers reach for by analogy.
바뀌다.explanation: "to change, to be switched" in Korean is 바뀌다 (bakkwida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 바뀌어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 바뀌다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 비밀번호가 바뀌었어요. ("The password changed.") — then reshape the same stem into 바뀌고 싶어요 (desire), 바뀔 수 있어요 (ability), and 바뀔 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
바뀌다.shortExplanation: 바뀌다 means "to change, to be switched" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 바뀌다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 바뀌어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 바뀌다 transitively — '번호를 바뀌었어요' is wrong because 바뀌다 has no object. If YOU did it, use 바꾸다: 번호를 바꿨어요.
Don't write the polite form as 바껴요 or the past as 바꼈어요; the 바뀌- stem keeps its 위 and gives 바뀌어요 / 바뀌었어요.
Don't blur 바뀌다 and 변하다: 마음이 바뀌었어요 = I changed my mind (switched decisions), but 마음이 변했어요 = my feelings have transformed (e.g., fallen out of love).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 바뀌다 becomes 바뀔 수 있어요 ("can") and 바뀔 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not change, to be switched.
I want to change, to be switched.
I can change, to be switched.
I have to change, to be switched.

usagePhrases.note: 바뀌다 = something gets switched/replaced by something else. The thing that changes takes 이/가, never 을/를.

examples.en: The meeting time got changed to 3 o'clock.
examples.note: Super common at work — schedules and times 'get changed' on you; note 3시로 with (으)로.

examples.en: Oh, the shop's name changed.
examples.note: ~네요 adds a 'huh, I just noticed' tone — natural the moment you spot a change.

examples.en: The plan might change again.
examples.note: 또 (again) + 바뀌다 is the everyday way to warn that things aren't fixed yet.

ex.en: After starting exercise, my day became different.
ex.note: Emphasizes that the whole feel is different now.

달라지다.nuance: 달라지다 spotlights the before-and-after gap: something is now clearly unlike how it used to be, which makes it the everyday verb for noticing change in a person's looks, mood, or a situation. It's the inchoative of the adjective 다르다 (to be different) — 다르 + -아지다 'become' — and that origin is the #1 pitfall: 다르다 states a static difference between two things (A는 B와 달라요 = A is different from B), while 달라지다 is the dynamic act of becoming different over time (분위기가 달라졌어요 = the mood changed). It overlaps with 변하다 and 바뀌다, but the dividing line is focus: 달라지다 = 'the result looks different now,' 변하다 = 'the inner nature transformed,' 바뀌다 = 'one thing got swapped for another.' Both 달라지다 and the thing changing take 이/가; the form 달라져요 comes from -지다 verbs taking 어 in the 요-form (지+어 → 져).
달라지다.explanation: 달라지다 (dallajida) = "to become different, to change". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 달라져요 plus one useful sentence like 분위기가 완전히 달라졌어요. ("The atmosphere became completely different."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 달라지고 싶어요 for what you want, 달라질 수 있어요 for what you can, 달라질 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
달라지다.shortExplanation: 달라지다 means "to become different, to change" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 달라지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 달라져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't confuse it with 다르다 — 다르다 is an adjective for a static difference (저는 형과 성격이 달라요), while 달라지다 is a verb for becoming different (성격이 달라졌어요).
It's intransitive, so don't attach 을/를: say 생각이 달라졌어요, not 생각을 달라졌어요. To deliberately change something, use 바꾸다.
Don't say the present as 달라요 when you mean 'is changing'; 달라요 = 'is different (now)', 달라지고 있어요 = 'is becoming different'.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 달라지다 becomes 달라질 수 있어요 ("can") and 달라질 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not become different, to change.
I want to become different, to change.
I can become different, to change.
I have to become different, to change.

usagePhrases.note: 달라지다 = end up noticeably different from before. Built from 다르다 (be different) + -아지다.

examples.en: Did you cut your hair? You look different.
examples.note: Great compliment-ish line — 느낌이 달라지다 = the vibe/impression changed.

examples.en: Now that I've lived here, my thinking has changed a lot.
examples.note: Use for gradual inner change — 생각이/가치관이 달라지다.

examples.en: The rules will be different starting next year.
examples.note: Common in notices about policies, fees, or schedules changing.

ex.en: After I started exercising, my stress decreased.

줄다.nuance: 줄다 is the exact opposite of 늘다 — it means an amount, number, or size gets smaller — and the two are learned as a pair (늘다/줄다). Like 늘다 it is a ㄹ-irregular verb, so the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다, giving the formal 줍니다 (not *줄습니다). The crucial synonym contrast is 줄다 vs 줄이다: 줄다 is intransitive — the thing shrinks by itself (소리가 줄었어요 = the sound got quieter on its own), while 줄이다 is the causative — you deliberately reduce something (소리를 줄였어요 = I turned the sound down). Its formal report-style synonym is 감소하다 (Sino-Korean 減少, 'reduce-decrease'), used for statistics; 줄다 is the natural conversational word. The English-speaker pitfall mirrors 늘다: don't say *줄습니다 (the ㄹ drops to make 줍니다), and don't put an object with 줄다. 'I reduced my spending' needs the transitive 줄이다 (지출을 줄였어요); 'my spending decreased' uses 줄다 with the subject particle (지출이 줄었어요).
줄다.explanation: 줄다 (julda) = "to decrease". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 줄어요 plus one useful sentence like 살이 줄었어요 ("I lost weight"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 줄고 싶어요 for what you want, 줄 수 있어요 for what you can, 줄 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
줄다.shortExplanation: 줄다 means "to decrease" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 줄다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 줄어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the formal form as 줄습니다 — the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다, so it is 줍니다.
Confusing 줄다 with 줄이다. 'The cost decreased' is 비용이 줄었어요 (by itself); 'I cut the cost' is 비용을 줄였어요 (you did it). 이/가 goes with 줄다, 을/를 with 줄이다.
Saying 살을 줄었어요 to mean 'I lost weight' — 줄다 takes no object, so it's 살이 줄었어요 (with 이). If you mean you deliberately slimmed, Koreans more often say 살을 뺐어요 (from 빼다).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 줄다 becomes 줄 수 있어요 ("can") and 줄 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 줄다 has an irregular stem (ㄹ). Memorize its polite form 줄어요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

examples.en: The shop's customers decreased a lot
examples.note: Simple drop in numbers, past tense

examples.en: Work has decreased lately so I'm a bit free
examples.note: -어서 ties the decrease to having free time

examples.en: My allowance is gradually shrinking
examples.note: -고 있어요 plus 점점 stresses a slow ongoing fall

ex.ko: 회사 일 때문에 한국에 살게 됐어요.
ex.en: Because of work, I ended up living in Korea.
ex.note: A classic circumstantial 게 되다 sentence.

살다.nuance: 살다 means 'to live' in two senses — to reside somewhere and to be alive — and is a ㄹ-irregular verb. The stem ㄹ disappears before ㅂ, ㄴ, and the honorific 시, producing 삽니다 (not 살읍니다), 사세요 (not 살으세요), and 사니까; before vowel endings the ㄹ stays, so the polite present is 살아요. For where you live, the default particle is the static-location 에: 서울에 살아요. Interestingly, because living is an activity carried out over time, the dynamic-location 에서 is also acceptable and common, especially with hopes and experiences (한국에서 살고 싶어요) — this is one of the few cases where both 에 and 에서 work with the same verb. Contrast 살다 with 거주하다 (居住하다, Sino-Korean 'to reside'), a stiff, formal/written word used on official forms (거주지 'place of residence'); in speech you always say 살다. The English-speaker pitfall is keeping the ㄹ to say 살읍니다 instead of 삽니다, and reflexively choosing 에서 for every location when plain residence prefers 에.
살다.explanation: 살다 (salda) means "to live". Start from the polite form 살아요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 살다. A strong first sentence is 서울에 살아요 ("I live in Seoul"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 살다 also becomes 살고 싶어요 (want), 살 수 있어요 (can), and 못 살아요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then bend it.
살다.shortExplanation: 살다 means "to live" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 살다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 살아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Keeping the ㄹ before consonant endings and saying 살읍니다 / 살으세요 — as a ㄹ-irregular it drops: 삽니다 and 사세요.
Always using 에서 for the place you live — for stating a plain address, the static 에 is standard: 서울에 살아요 (에서 leans toward an active life-experience).
Using the formal 거주하다 in casual conversation — it sounds like a government form; everyday speech uses 살다.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 살다 becomes 살 수 있어요 ("can") and 살 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem: ㄹ
conjugationTips.body: 살다 is a ㄹ-stem word. The ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ endings: 살다 → 삽니다 (formal), 사는 (describing a noun), 사세요 (honorific). Before a vowel the ㄹ stays: 살아요.

usagePhrases.note: the place of residence takes 에 (static location), not 에서

examples.en: I live in Seoul now.
examples.note: residence with 에; 지금 'now' marks current address

examples.en: My parents live in Busan.
examples.note: honorific 사세요 for elders — note the ㄹ has dropped

examples.en: Someday I want to live on Jeju.
examples.note: future hope; 에서 + 살다 frames it as a life to be lived there

ex.en: Because of work, I suddenly ended up moving.

이사하다.nuance: 이사하다 specifically means relocating your residence — changing the home you live in — built from Sino-Korean 移徙 (移 'shift', 徙 'relocate') plus 하다. Contrast it sharply with 옮기다, which is just physically moving an object from one spot to another (책상을 옮기다 'move the desk'); you never use 옮기다 for changing homes, and you never use 이사하다 for shifting furniture. It splits into 이사 가다 (move away, focus on departure) and 이사 오다 (move in, focus on arrival near the speaker). Being a 하다-verb, the negative wraps the noun: 이사 안 해요 / 이사 못 해요, NOT 안 이사해요. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is treating it like English 'move' as a transitive verb — Koreans don't say '집을 이사해요'; the home is implied, so just 이사해요 is complete.
이사하다.explanation: 이사하다 (isahada) = "to move house". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 이사해요 plus one useful sentence like 이사 가다 ("to move away (to a new place)"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 이사하고 싶어요 for what you want, 이사할 수 있어요 for what you can, 이사 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests.
이사하다.shortExplanation: 이사하다 means "to move house" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 이사하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 이사해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 안 이사해요 — for 하다-compound verbs the negation goes inside, so the correct form is 이사 안 해요 (and 이사 못 해요 for inability).
Saying 집을 이사해요 by direct-translating 'move house' — 이사하다 already contains the idea of home, so the object is dropped; just say 이사해요.
Using 옮기다 for relocating yourself (e.g. 서울로 옮겼어요) — 옮기다 is only for moving objects; for changing residence use 서울로 이사했어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 이사하다 becomes 이사할 수 있어요 ("can") and 이사할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: to move away (to a new place)
usagePhrases.note: 이사 가다 stresses leaving toward a destination; pairs with 로/으로 for where you go

examples.en: I'm moving next month.
examples.note: Bare 이사해요 already implies changing homes; no extra object needed

examples.ko: 집이 좁아서 더 넓은 곳으로 이사하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: jibi jobaseo deo neolbeun goseuro isahago sipeoyo.
examples.en: The house is cramped, so I want to move somewhere bigger.
examples.note: Destination 'somewhere bigger' takes 으로, the direction particle

examples.ko: 이번 주말에 이사하는데 좀 도와줄 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: ibeon jumare isahaneunde jom dowajul su isseoyo?
examples.en: I'm moving this weekend, could you help out a bit?
examples.note: -는데 sets up the situation before the request — natural spoken framing

맡다.en: to take charge of; to be assigned

ex.en: I ended up taking charge of a new task.
ex.note: Good for work or school responsibilities.

맡다.nuance: 맡다 is the everyday native-Korean verb for taking on a role or responsibility — a task, a project, a part, even a saved seat. It feels more personal and active than the Sino-Korean 담당하다: where 담당하다 is the official 'assigned to me' on an org chart, 맡다 is the warm, often-volunteered 'I'll take this', so 제가 맡을게요 sounds team-friendly and proactive in a meeting. Crucial spelling and conjugation point: the stem ends in ㅌ, and it is a plain regular verb, NOT a ㄷ-irregular — so it stays 맡아요 / 맡았어요 / 맡을게요, and learners who mistakenly 'soften' the ㅌ to ㄹ (마라요, 마랐어요) are simply wrong. Its causative partner 맡기다 ('to entrust/hand over') flips the direction: you 맡다 a job yourself, but you 맡기다 it to someone else (저한테 맡기세요). Habitual collocations: 역할을 맡다, 책임을 맡다, 업무를 맡다, 자리를 맡다.
맡다.explanation: 맡다 (matda) means "to take charge of (be assigned)". Start from the polite form 맡아요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 맡다. A strong first sentence is 역할을 맡다 ("to take on a role"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 맡다 also becomes 맡고 싶어요 (want), 맡을 수 있어요 (can), and 맡을 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then bend it.
맡다.shortExplanation: 맡다 means "to take charge of (be assigned)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 맡다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 맡아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Not a ㄷ-irregular: the stem is 맡- (ㅌ), so it conjugates 맡아요 / 맡았어요, never 마라요 / 마랐어요. Don't soften the ㅌ.
Don't confuse 맡다 (you take the task on) with its causative 맡기다 (you hand the task to someone else): 제가 맡을게요 vs. 저한테 맡기세요 are opposite directions.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 맡다 becomes 맡을 수 있어요 ("can") and 맡을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not take charge of (be assigned).
I want to take charge of (be assigned).
I can take charge of (be assigned).
I have to take charge of (be assigned).

usagePhrases.note: 역할(役割) 'role'; 맡다 collocates with roles, parts, and duties you personally accept.

examples.en: I'll take that on.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ게요 = a willing commitment to the listener; sounds proactive and reliable.

examples.en: Assistant Manager Kim took charge of this event.
examples.note: Past 맡았어요 (stem ㅌ + 아) reports who got the assignment — note it is NOT 마랐어요.

examples.en: The department head entrusted me with that project.
examples.note: 맡기다 = causative 'hand over/entrust'; 저한테 marks the receiver — contrast with plain 맡다.

ex.en: These days I have come to sleep earlier.

일찍.nuance: 일찍 means 'early' in the sense of an EARLY POINT IN TIME — early hour of the day or ahead of a schedule — and is the natural opposite of 늦게(late). The classic confusion is 일찍 vs 빨리: 일찍 is about WHEN on the clock (일찍 일어나요 = 'wake up at an early hour'), while 빨리 is about SPEED/quickness (빨리 일어나요 = 'get up quick!'). So '일찍 오세요' invites someone to arrive at an early time, whereas '빨리 오세요' urges them to hurry. It pairs habitually with 자다, 일어나다, 출근하다, 도착하다, 출발하다. Register-neutral and polite-safe. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 일찍/빨리 mix-up, since English 'early' and 'fast/quick' feel adjacent but map to two different Korean adverbs; also remember 일찍 is an adverb already, so you never conjugate it like the adjective 이르다.
일찍.explanation: "early" is 일찍 (iljjik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 일찍 자요 ("I sleep early"). Watch the particle attached to 일찍 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
일찍.shortExplanation: 일찍 means "early" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 빨리 when you mean 'at an early hour'. 빨리 자요 means 'sleep quickly'; to say 'sleep early (in the evening)' use 일찍 자요.
Trying to conjugate it as if it were an adjective. 일찍 is the fixed adverb; you don't say 일찍어요. The related adjective is 이르다 ('to be early').
Word order: 와요 일찍 mirrors English; Korean puts the adverb first — 일찍 와요.

examples.en: I usually sleep early.
examples.note: Simple: 일찍 = at an early hour, before 자요.

examples.en: Tomorrow I want to get up early.
examples.note: Everyday: 일찍 + 일어나다 is the standard 'wake up early' collocation.

examples.en: Worried about traffic, I left thirty minutes early.
examples.note: Real situation: 일찍 here means 'ahead of schedule', and 30분 일찍 = 'earlier by 30 min'.

cluster.title: 빨리 vs 일찍 vs 어서
cluster.rule: 빨리 is about speed and 일찍 is about the clock: 빨리 오세요 means 'get here quick', 일찍 오세요 means 'come at an early hour'. 어서 also pushes for speed but sounds warm and welcoming, so it lives in polite invitations like 어서 오세요.

members.hint: about speed, and can sound impatient
about the clock, not the speed
warm urging, mostly with polite invitations

ex.en: I decided to sleep early starting today.
ex.note: 자다 becomes 자기로 in the decision pattern.

자다.nuance: 자다 becomes 잘 before some future or ability forms: 잘 거예요, 잘 수 있어요.
자다.explanation: "to sleep" in Korean is 자다 (jada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 자요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 자다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 잘 자요 ("sleep well / good night.") — then reshape the same stem into 자고 싶어요 (desire), 잘 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 자요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
자다.shortExplanation: 자다 means "to sleep" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 자다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 자요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
자 주세요 is grammatically possible, but 잘 자요 is the natural phrase for “good night.” Use request forms only with a real context.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 자다 becomes 잘 수 있어요 ("can") and 잘 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

examples.en: I sleep early today.
examples.note: Daily routine.

examples.en: I could not sleep well yesterday.
examples.note: Common complaint.

examples.en: Shall we sleep now?
examples.note: Suggestion.

ex.en: After exercising, my body felt lighter.
ex.note: 몸 is the subject of the changed state.

몸.nuance: 몸 is the physical body taken as a whole, and crucially it's also the word Koreans reach for to describe how they FEEL: 몸이 아파요 (sick) and 몸이 안 좋아요 (off/unwell) are the everyday health phrases. The near-synonym is the Sino-Korean 신체(身體, 'body-substance'), but 신체 is clinical/official — 신체검사 (physical exam), 신체 활동 (physical activity) — and sounds stiff if you use it about yourself, so say 몸. Habitual collocations: 몸이 아프다, 몸이 안 좋다, 몸이 피곤하다, 몸이 무겁다, 몸조심하다, 몸이 약하다 (to have a weak constitution). The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle and the verb: you say 몸이 아프다 ('the body is sick'), so the body is the SUBJECT (이/가) — never 몸을 아파요. Also don't directly translate 'my body is heavy' as a weight statement; 몸이 무겁다 means you feel sluggish/lethargic, not that you weigh a lot.
몸.explanation: 몸 (mom) = "body". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 몸이 아파요 ("I feel sick (lit. my body hurts)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 몸, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.
몸.shortExplanation: 몸 means "body" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 몸을 아파요 with the object particle 을. 아프다 is an adjective-like stative verb, so the body is the subject: 몸이 아파요.
Using 신체 in casual speech, e.g. 신체가 아파요. That sounds like a medical chart; everyday Korean is 몸이 아파요.
Reading 몸이 무거워요 as 'I'm overweight.' It means you feel heavy/sluggish; weight gain is 살이 쪘어요.

usagePhrases.en: I feel sick (lit. my body hurts)
usagePhrases.note: the default way to say you're unwell; note the particle 이, not 을
softer/vaguer than 아파요; good for general malaise or even feeling low
set farewell when it's cold or someone's sick; 몸 + 조심하다 fused

usagePhrases.en: I feel sluggish (lit. my body is heavy)
usagePhrases.note: tiredness/heaviness, not literal weight; contrast 살이 쪘어요 for weight

examples.en: I'm a bit tired today.
examples.note: simple: 몸이 + adjective is the basic frame for how your body feels

examples.en: I was sick, so I couldn't go to work.
examples.note: everyday: 아파서 (A-아서) gives the reason; pair with 못 가다

examples.ko: 요즘 무리해서 그런지 몸이 자꾸 안 좋아요.

examples.en: Maybe because I've been overdoing it, I keep feeling under the weather lately.
examples.note: real-life: 안 좋다 for ongoing vague unwellness, 자꾸 = keeps happening

ex.en: My body felt lighter.

가볍다.nuance: 가볍다 means light in weight (가벼운 가방), and figuratively 'light' in many senses: 마음이 가볍다 (heart is light/relieved), 가벼운 감기 (a mild cold), 가벼운 농담 (a light joke), 가볍게 운동하다 (to exercise lightly), and even negatively 입이 가볍다 ('light-mouthed' = can't keep a secret, the exact opposite of 입이 무겁다). It is the opposite of 무겁다 (heavy). Conjugation is the ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우 before a vowel ending, so 가벼워요 and the modifier 가벼운 — the same pattern as 무겁다→무거워, 춥다→추워. A synonym note: 가볍다 covers 'light/mild', but 'easy' (simple to do) is 쉽다, so 'an easy question' is 쉬운 문제, not 가벼운 문제 — though 가벼운 문제 can mean a 'minor/trivial' issue. Be careful too that 'light' as in brightness/color is 밝다 (밝은 색 = a light/bright color), not 가볍다. It collocates with 가방·노트북·옷·마음·발걸음·농담·감기. English-speaker pitfall: writing 가볍어요 instead of 가벼워요, and stretching 가볍다 to cover 'easy' (use 쉽다) or 'light-colored' (use 밝다).
가볍다.explanation: "light (in weight)" is 가볍다 (gabyeopda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가벼워요 ("it is light"). Watch the particle attached to 가볍다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
가볍다.shortExplanation: 가볍다 means "light (in weight)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 가볍어요 instead of 가벼워요 — 가볍다 is ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ becomes 우 before the ending (가볍 + 어요 → 가벼워요).
Using 가볍다 for 'easy to do' (이 문제는 가벼워요 meaning simple) — 'easy' is 쉽다: 이 문제는 쉬워요. 가볍다 is weight or 'minor', not difficulty.
Using 가볍다 for a light/pale color (가벼운 색) — a light color is 밝은 색 (밝다 = bright); 가볍다 only refers to weight or figurative lightness.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우, then 어요 → 가벼워요
ㅂ-irregular modifier: ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ (가볍 → 가벼운)

examples.en: This laptop is really light.
examples.note: ㅂ-irregular: 가볍 + 어요 → ㅂ to 우 → 가벼워요, not 가볍어요.

examples.en: I bought one light bag.
examples.note: The ㅂ-irregular modifier 가벼운 (ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ) precedes 가방.

examples.en: Today my heart feels much lighter.
examples.note: 마음이 가볍다 = to feel relieved/unburdened — a common figurative use.

해요체.nuance: 해요체 is polite conversation, not formal ceremony language. It sounds warmer and more natural than 합쇼체 in daily life.
해요체.explanation: 해요체 (haeyoche) = "everyday polite speech style". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 발표 끝났어요. ("The presentation is over.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 해요체, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
해요체.shortExplanation: 해요체 means "everyday polite speech style" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 합쇼체 with classmates after class can sound stiff or distant.
Using 반말 with someone you just met can sound rude even if the grammar is simple.

usagePhrases.note: Natural polite everyday style after the formal presentation is done.

usagePhrases.en: May I ask the teacher a question?

examples.ko: 친구가 아니면 처음에는 해요체로 말하는 게 안전해요.

합쇼체.nuance: 합쇼체 overlaps with the name 하십시오체. Learners mainly need to recognize the endings -ㅂ니다/습니다, -ㅂ니까/습니까, and -(으)십시오.
합쇼체.explanation: 합쇼체 (hapsyoche) means "formal polite speech style". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 지금부터 발표를 시작하겠습니다. ("I will begin the presentation now."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 합쇼체 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
합쇼체.shortExplanation: 합쇼체 means "formal polite speech style" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 합쇼체 everywhere because it feels 'more polite'. In everyday talk, it can sound too stiff.
Forgetting that ㄹ drops before ㅂ니다: 살다 becomes 삽니다.

usagePhrases.en: I will begin the presentation now.

examples.en: In an interview, speaking in formal polite style sounds natural.
examples.note: A real setting where 합쇼체 fits.

반말.nuance: 반말 is not 'bad Korean'. It is the right style in close relationships, but the wrong style in many public or first-meeting settings.
반말.explanation: "casual non-polite speech" is 반말 (banmal). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 우리 반말해도 돼요? ("Can we speak casually to each other?"). Watch the particle attached to 반말 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
반말.shortExplanation: 반말 means "casual non-polite speech" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 반말 with a teacher or staff member because the learner knows the short form.
Thinking 반말 equals friendly in every situation. Relationship and permission matter.

usagePhrases.en: Can we speak casually to each other?
usagePhrases.note: A common way to ask permission before switching.

usagePhrases.en: I use casual speech with close friends.

examples.ko: 처음 만난 사람에게 반말을 쓰면 무례하게 들릴 수 있어요.

examples.en: If you use casual speech with someone you just met, it can sound rude.
examples.note: Social boundary.

ex.en: At first, speak politely.

존댓말.nuance: 존댓말 is about social respect. It does not automatically mean the most formal ending possible.
존댓말.explanation: 존댓말 (jondaenmal) = "polite or respectful speech". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 처음에는 존댓말로 말하세요. ("At first, speak politely.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 존댓말, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
존댓말.shortExplanation: 존댓말 means "polite or respectful speech" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Equating 존댓말 only with 합니다. 해요체 is also 존댓말.
Using honorific -(으)시- for yourself. Respectful speech and subject honorifics are related but not identical.

usagePhrases.en: I use polite speech with the teacher.

examples.ko: 존댓말을 써도 상황에 따라 해요체와 합쇼체가 달라져요.

examples.en: Even when using polite speech, haeyo style and formal style differ by situation.

말투.nuance: 말투 can describe grammar level, but also attitude. A sentence can be grammatically polite and still sound cold or awkward.
말투.explanation: 말투 (maltu) means "way of speaking; speech tone". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 어떤 말투를 써야 해요? ("What way of speaking should I use?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 말투 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
말투.shortExplanation: 말투 means "way of speaking; speech tone" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking only the verb ending matters. Particles, word choice, and directness also affect 말투.

usagePhrases.en: What way of speaking should I use?

examples.ko: 발표에서는 말투를 조금 더 격식 있게 바꿔야 해요.
examples.romanization: balpyoeseoneun maltureul jogeum deo gyeoksik itge bakkwoya haeyo.
examples.en: In a presentation, you need to make your tone a little more formal.

ex.en: An interview is a formal setting.

격식.nuance: 격식 is not just politeness. It is the formal frame expected by the setting.
격식.explanation: "formality; formal manners" is 격식 (gyeoksik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 격식 있는 자리 ("a formal setting"). Watch the particle attached to 격식 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
격식.shortExplanation: 격식 means "formality; formal manners" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 격식 있는 말투 with close friends can sound distant or theatrical.

usagePhrases.note: A key phrase for choosing 합쇼체.

examples.ko: 면접은 격식 있는 자리라서 합쇼체가 자연스러워요.

examples.en: An interview is a formal setting, so formal polite style sounds natural.
examples.note: Connects setting to speech level.

ex.en: I will begin the presentation now.

발표.nuance: 발표(發表)는 '필 발 + 겉 표', 곧 '안에 있던 것을 겉으로 드러내 알림'이라는 뜻으로, 여러 사람 앞에서 자기 생각이나 조사한 내용을 말로 알리는 것을 가리켜요. 비슷한 '연설'은 정치인·대표가 청중에게 행하는 더 공식적이고 일방적인 말하기라 학교 과제에는 안 어울리고, '공지'는 '날짜·결과를 알리는 통보'라 말로 설명하는 발표와 다르며, '보고'는 윗사람에게 결과를 전달하는 데 초점이 있어요. 그래서 학생이 수업에서 하는 것은 '발표'가 딱 맞아요. '발표하다' 동사와 '발표를 하다' 형태가 둘 다 자연스럽고, '발표 준비/자료/순서'와 잘 어울려요. 한 가지 더, '합격자 발표'처럼 결과를 공표한다는 뜻도 있어 영어 announce와 겹치지만, 수업 맥락에서는 말로 설명하는 presentation을 뜻한다는 점을 구분하세요.
발표.explanation: 발표 (balpyo) = "presentation, announcing (in class)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 발표를 하다 ("give a presentation") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 발표, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.
발표.shortExplanation: 발표 means "presentation, announcing (in class)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'발표를 말하다'는 같은 뜻을 두 번 말한 겹말이라 어색해요. '발표를 하다' 또는 '발표하다'면 충분합니다.
'발표' 자체가 동사 '발표하다'로 쓰이니 'I will presentation'처럼 영어식으로 '발표할 거예요'를 빼먹고 명사만 던지면 문장이 안 돼요. 동사형을 꼭 붙이세요.
결과를 알리는 '합격자 발표'와 수업의 '구두 발표'를 같은 말로 뭉뚱그리지 마세요. 맥락에 따라 announce인지 oral presentation인지 구분해야 의미가 분명합니다.

usagePhrases.note: 발표 + 준비로 미리 갖추는 일을 가리켜요

examples.en: I finished preparing my presentation yesterday.
examples.note: '다'는 '남김없이/모두'라는 뜻의 부사예요.

examples.en: I'm so nervous about presenting in front of people.
examples.note: '-(으)려니까'는 '~하려고 하니까'로 의도와 그에 따른 심정을 이어요.

ex.en: In an interview, I speak clearly in polite speech.

면접.nuance: 면접 (面接, 'face-contact/meet') literally means meeting face-to-face, and refers to the job interview where you sit before evaluators. The most important thing to lock in is the FIXED verb: 면접을 보다, literally 'to see an interview,' which uses the same 보다 as 시험을 보다 (take a test) — Korean treats undergoing an evaluation as 'seeing' it. The synonym contrast: 면접 is the oral, face-to-face interview, while 시험 (試驗) is a written test/exam, and 면담 (面談) is a softer counseling-style talk (e.g., with a professor), not a hiring screen. After a 면접 you hope to 합격하다 (pass) rather than 떨어지다 (fall/fail) or 불합격하다. Register: neutral, used in any job-search context. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 하다: 면접을 하다 sounds off from the candidate's side — you 면접을 보다 (take it); the company that conducts it may 면접을 진행하다. Also note you pass 면접에 (with 에), patterning like 시험에 합격하다.
면접.explanation: 면접 (myeonjeop) = "job interview". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 면접을 보다 ("to have a job interview") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 면접, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.
면접.shortExplanation: 면접 means "job interview" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 면접을 하다 as the candidate. The fixed verb is 면접을 보다 (just like 시험을 보다).
Confusing 면접 (oral, face-to-face interview) with 시험 (a written exam). Different formats, different prep.
Using 를 with 합격: 면접을 합격하다 is wrong. You pass INTO it with 에 → 면접에 합격하다.

usagePhrases.note: 보다 'to see' is the FIXED verb here, exactly like 시험을 보다 (take an exam).
합격하다 (合格, pass) + 에 marking the interview you pass; opposite is 떨어지다 (fail).
면접 + 준비 (準備, preparation) — getting ready for the interview.
1차 (1次, first round); Korean hiring often has 1차, 2차 면접 stages.

examples.en: I have a job interview tomorrow.

examples.en: I prepared hard for the interview.

examples.en: I'm so happy I passed the interview.
examples.note: 면접에 합격하다 + ~아서 (reason) + 기쁘다 (glad).

ex.en: The way of speaking changes depending on the situation.

상황.nuance: 상황 (狀況, '狀 condition/form + 況 circumstances' — the configuration of circumstances) describes the overall set of conditions surrounding a moment or event, broader than a single 경우 (a specific case or instance — 이런 경우 = 'in this one case', vs 이런 상황 = 'in this whole situation'). The reflexive phrase 상황에 따라(서) 다르다 ('it depends on the situation') is one of the most useful hedges in Korean, and 이런/그런 상황에서 sets up advice or reactions. Register is neutral. Two pitfalls: keep 상황 (the circumstances around an event) distinct from 상태 (狀態, the state/condition of a single thing or body — 건강 상태 'health condition', 배터리 상태 'battery state'); you describe a person's mood with a 상태, but the events around them with a 상황. And use 에 따라 (not 으로) for 'depending on': 상황에 따라, never 상황으로.
상황.explanation: "situation, circumstances" is 상황 (sanghwang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 현재 상황 ("the current situation"). Watch the particle attached to 상황 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
상황.shortExplanation: 상황 means "situation, circumstances" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 상황 (the situation/circumstances around an event) with 상태 (the state or condition of a thing or body): 건강 상태, not 건강 상황.
Use 에 따라 for 'depending on the situation', not 으로: 상황에 따라(서), never 상황으로.
For one specific instance, 경우 is sharper than 상황: '이런 경우' = 'in this particular case' vs '이런 상황' = 'in this whole situation'.

usagePhrases.note: 상황 follows a noun/modifier naming the state of affairs
상황이 좋다/나쁘다/심각하다 describe how things stand; subject takes 이/가
frames advice or a reaction to a set of conditions
상황에 따라(서) 다르다 = it depends on the situation

examples.en: How's the situation right now?
examples.note: Simple: 상황 with 이/가 asking after the state of things

examples.ko: 이런 상황에서는 어떻게 해야 할지 모르겠어요.
examples.romanization: ireon sanghwangeseoneun eotteoke haeya halji moreugesseoyo.
examples.en: In a situation like this, I don't know what I should do.

끝나다.nuance: 끝나다 means 'to end / be over / finish' as something that happens by itself — it is intransitive, so the thing that ends takes the subject marker 이/가: 수업이 끝나요, past 끝났어요 (끝나 + 았어요). The essential pairing is with its transitive twin 끝내다 ('to finish/end something'), used when a person actively brings an action to a close with an object: 저는 일을 끝내요 ('I finish the work', 을/를). This 끝나다 (happens) vs 끝내다 (someone does it) split mirrors 시작하다 family logic and is one of Korean's classic intransitive/transitive verb pairs (like 켜지다/켜다, 열리다/열다). The natural opposite is 시작하다 ('to begin'). A nuance of completion: 다 끝났어요 ('it's all done') is the everyday way to announce something is finished, and 끝 alone is an interjection meaning 'the end'. The English-speaker pitfall is using 끝나다 with an object — saying 일을 끝나요 by analogy to English 'I end the work' — when an actor finishes something it must be the transitive 일을 끝내요.
끝나다.explanation: 끝나다 (kkeutnada) means "to end". Start from the polite form 끝나요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 끝나다. A strong first sentence is 수업이 끝나요 ("the class ends"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 끝나다 also becomes 끝나고 싶어요 (want), 끝날 수 있어요 (can), and 못 끝나요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then bend it.
끝나다.shortExplanation: 끝나다 means "to end" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 끝나다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 끝나요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 끝나다 with an object (일을 끝나요) — 끝나다 is intransitive; when a person finishes something, use the transitive 끝내다: 일을 끝내요.
Marking the thing that ends with 을/를 (수업을 끝나요) — it takes the subject marker: 수업이 끝나요.
Mixing up the past forms — 끝나다 → 끝났어요 (it ended on its own) vs 끝내다 → 끝냈어요 (I finished it); pick the one that matches whether there is a doer.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 끝나다 becomes 끝날 수 있어요 ("can") and 끝날 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: intransitive: the thing that ends takes 이/가

examples.en: Class ends at three.
examples.note: time at 에; intransitive 수업이

examples.en: Work ended early today.
examples.note: the event ends on its own, so 일이 (이/가)

examples.ko: 이 일만 끝내면 집에 갈 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: i ilman kkeunnaemyeon jibe gal su isseoyo.
examples.en: Once I finish just this task I can go home.
examples.note: real plan: a doer finishes it, so the transitive 끝내다

cluster.title: 끝나다 vs 마치다
cluster.rule: Ask who does the ending. If the thing ends on its own, use 끝나다 with 이/가 (수업이 끝났어요). If a person brings it to a close, the everyday word is 끝내다 with 을/를 (일을 끝냈어요). 마치다 is the more formal, "properly concluded" version of that — 오늘 일을 마쳤어요 — and you'll also hear it on its own (수업 마치고 갈게요), so treat it as the polished option rather than the default.

members.hint: it ends by itself — takes 이/가

members.when: you bring something to a close
members.hint: the formal "finish it" — everyday word is 끝내다

ex.ko: 선생님에 대해 말할 때는 높임말을 써요.
ex.en: When talking about a teacher, I use honorific language.
ex.note: The honored person can be the person being discussed.

높임말.nuance: 높임말 is not only being polite to the listener. It can honor a third person, such as a teacher or parent.
높임말.explanation: 높임말 (nopimmal) = "honorific or respectful language". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 높임말을 쓰다 ("to use honorific language") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 높임말, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
높임말.shortExplanation: 높임말 means "honorific or respectful language" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using -(으)시- for yourself. Do not say 제가 가세요.
Thinking 존댓말 and 높임말 are always the same. They overlap, but they answer different social questions.

examples.ko: 선생님에 대해 말할 때는 높임말을 써요.
examples.romanization: seonsaengnime daehae malhal ttaeneun nopimmareul sseoyo.
examples.en: When talking about a teacher, I use honorific language.
examples.note: The honored person is the topic of the sentence.

ex.en: The teacher is coming.
ex.note: The teacher is the respected subject.

께서.nuance: 께서 honors the subject. It is not the same as 께, which means 'to' a respected person.
께서.explanation: 께서 (kkeseo) means "honorific subject particle". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 선생님께서 오세요. ("The teacher is coming."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 께서 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
께서.shortExplanation: 께서 means "honorific subject particle" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 께서 for yourself: 제가께서 is impossible.
Confusing 께서 with 께. 선생님께서 오세요 but 선생님께 말씀드려요.

usagePhrases.note: Particle and verb both carry respect.

examples.en: The boss is in the meeting room.
examples.note: Respected subject plus 계시다.

ex.en: I contact my parents.

께.nuance: 께 marks a respected recipient. 께서 marks a respected subject.
께.explanation: "to a respected person" is 께 (kke). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 선생님께 질문해요. ("I ask the teacher a question."). Watch the particle attached to 께 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
께.shortExplanation: 께 means "to a respected person" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 선생님께서 질문해요 when you mean 'I ask the teacher'. Use 선생님께 질문해요.
Using 한테 in formal respectful contexts where 께 is expected.

usagePhrases.en: I ask the teacher a question.

examples.en: I will first guide the customer.
examples.note: Formal service language.

ex.en: The teacher drinks coffee.
ex.note: Honors the person eating or drinking.

드시다.nuance: 드시다 honors the eater/drinker. It does not honor the food.
드시다.explanation: 드시다 (deusida) means "to eat; to drink (honorific)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 식사하셨어요? ("Have you eaten?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 드시다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
드시다.shortExplanation: 드시다 means "to eat; to drink (honorific)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 드시다 for your own eating: 제가 드세요 is wrong.
Thinking 드시다 means only 'eat'. It can also be used for drinking.

examples.en: Grandmother is eating.
examples.note: Traditional respectful meal word plus honorific verb.

ex.en: My parents sleep early.

주무시다.nuance: 주무시다 is a special honorific verb. Do not build it mechanically from 자다.
주무시다.explanation: "to sleep (honorific)" is 주무시다 (jumusida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 안녕히 주무세요. ("Good night. / Sleep well."). Watch the particle attached to 주무시다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
주무시다.shortExplanation: 주무시다 means "to sleep (honorific)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 자세요 can be understandable, but 주무세요 is the standard respectful form.
Using 주무시다 for yourself.

examples.en: My parents usually sleep early.
examples.note: Respectful family sentence.

ex.en: The teacher spoke.

말씀하시다.nuance: 말씀하시다 honors the speaker. 말씀드리다 humbles your act of telling someone respected.
말씀하시다.explanation: 말씀하시다 (malsseumhasida) = "to say; to speak (honorific)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 선생님께서 말씀하셨어요. ("The teacher said it.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 말씀하시다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
말씀하시다.shortExplanation: 말씀하시다 means "to say; to speak (honorific)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 말씀하시다 and 말씀드리다. The direction of respect is different.
Using 말하다 where 말씀하시다 is expected for a respected subject.

examples.en: My mother spoke first.
examples.note: Honors mother as subject.

ex.en: I will contact my parents first.

부모님.nuance: 부모님 is Sino-Korean 父母 ('father' 父 + 'mother' 母) plus the honorific suffix 님, so the respect is baked into the word itself and it is the everyday polite default — there is no need to add anything to make it courteous. The bare root 부모 exists but is abstract and institutional ('부모의 역할' the role of parents, '부모 교육' parenting education); aimed at a real person it sounds cold, so for your own or anyone's parents you say 부모님. Because 님 marks the referent as worthy of respect, every verb around it must climb to its honorific tier: 있다→계시다, 주다→드리다, 집→댁, 에게→께, and the topic/subject can even take 께서. The classic English-speaker pitfall is pairing 부모님 with plain verbs ('부모님이 있어요', '부모님한테 줬어요'); grammatically the words exist, but to a Korean ear it clashes like saying 'Her Majesty ate fast' — you must use 계세요 and 드렸어요/께.
부모님.explanation: "parents" is 부모님 (bumonim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 우리 부모님 ("my parents"). Watch the particle attached to 부모님 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
부모님.shortExplanation: 부모님 means "parents" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 부모 instead of 부모님 for an actual person ('제 부모는…') — without 님 it sounds blunt and textbook-like; always use 부모님 for real parents.
Using plain 있어요/없어요 with 부모님 ('부모님이 있어요') — the honorific subject demands 계세요/안 계세요.
Writing 부모님한테 or 부모님에게 — with the honorific 님 the dative must rise to 부모님께.

usagePhrases.note: 우리 + the built-in honorific 님 = the polite default
use 계시다, the honorific of 있다, to match 님
께 is the honorific of 에게/한테, required by 님
댁 is the honorific of 집 (house)
